{{short description|Collection of sets in which every two sets have the same intersection}}
{{other uses|sunflower (disambiguation)}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs1}}
{{unsolved|mathematics|For any sunflower size, does every set of uniformly sized sets which is of cardinality greater than some exponential in the set size contain a sunflower?}}
[[File:Sunflower (mathematics).svg|thumb|upright=1.2|A mathematical sunflower can be pictured as a flower. The ''kernel'' is the brown part, the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of every pair of sets. Each set of the sunflower is the [[union (set theory)|union]] of a petal and the kernel.]]
In the mathematical fields of [[set theory]] and [[extremal combinatorics]], a '''sunflower''' or '''<math>\Delta</math>-system'''<ref>The original term for this concept was "<math>\Delta</math>-system". More recently the term "sunflower", possibly introduced by {{harvtxt|Deza|Frankl|1981}}, has been gradually replacing it.</ref> is a collection of [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] in which the [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of any two distinct sets is the same. This common intersection is called the '''kernel''' of the sunflower.

The naming arises from a visual similarity to the botanical sunflower, arising when a [[Venn diagram]] of a sunflower set is arranged in an intuitive way. Suppose the shared elements of a sunflower set are clumped together at the centre of the diagram, and the nonshared elements are distributed in a circular pattern around the shared elements. Then when the Venn diagram is completed, the lobe-shaped subsets, which encircle the common elements and one or more unique elements, take on the appearance of the petals of a flower.

The main [[research question]] arising in relation to sunflowers is: under what conditions does there exist a ''large'' sunflower (a sunflower with many sets) in a given collection of sets? The '''<math>\Delta</math>-lemma''', '''sunflower lemma''', and the '''Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture''' give successively weaker conditions which would imply the existence of a large sunflower in a given collection, with the latter being one of the most famous open problems of extremal combinatorics.<ref name="kalai">{{Cite web|url=https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/2008/09/28/extremal-combinatorics-iii-some-basic-theorems/|title=Extremal Combinatorics III: Some Basic Theorems|website=Combinatorics and more|date=28 September 2008 |access-date=2021-12-10}}</ref>

== Formal definition ==

Suppose  <math>W</math> is a [[set system]] over <math>U</math>, that is, a collection of [[subset]]s of a set <math>U</math>. The collection <math>W</math> is a ''sunflower'' (or ''<math>\Delta</math>-system'') if there is a subset <math>S</math> of <math>U</math> such that for each [[Distinct (mathematics)|distinct]] <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> in <math>W</math>, we have <math>A \cap B = S</math>. In other words, a set system or collection of sets <math>W</math> is a sunflower if all sets in <math>W</math> share the same common subset of elements.

An element in <math>U</math> is either found in the common subset <math>S</math> or else appears in at most one of the <math>W</math> elements. No element of <math>U</math> is shared by just '''some''' of the <math>W</math> subsets, but not others.

=== Basic examples ===
If <math>W</math> contains 0, 1, or 2 subsets, then it is vacuously a sunflower. 

If <math>W</math> contains disjoint subsets, then it is a sunflower, with an [[Empty set|empty]] kernel.

== Sunflower lemma and conjecture ==

The study of sunflowers generally focuses on when set systems contain sunflowers, in particular, when a set system is sufficiently large to necessarily contain a sunflower.

Specifically, researchers analyze the function <math>f(k,r)</math> for nonnegative [[integer]]s <math>k, r</math>, which is defined to be the smallest nonnegative [[integer]] <math>n</math> such that, for any set system <math>W</math> such that every set <math>S \in W</math> has cardinality at most <math>k</math>, if <math>W</math> has more than <math>n</math> sets, then <math>W</math> contains a sunflower of <math>r</math> sets. Though it is not obvious that such an <math>n</math> must exist, a basic and simple result of [[Paul Erdős|Erdős]] and [[Richard Rado|Rado]], the Delta System Theorem, indicates that it does.

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = For each <math>k>0</math>, <math>r>0</math>, there is an integer <math>f(k,r)</math> such that if a set system <math>F</math> of <math>k</math>-sets is of cardinality greater than <math>f(k,r)</math>, then <math>F</math> contains a sunflower of size <math>r</math>.
| name = Erdős-Rado Delta System Theorem
| note = corollary of the sunflower lemma
}}

An alternative to <math>f(k,r)</math> is sometimes used, <math>Sun(k,r)</math>, where <math>f(k,r) = Sun(k,r) - 1</math>. This is the same as saying if <math>F</math> is of cardinality greater than or equal to <math>Sun(k,r)</math>, then <math>F</math> contains a sunflower of size <math>r</math>.

In the literature, <math>W</math> is often assumed to be a set rather than a collection, so any set can appear in <math>W</math> at most once. By adding dummy elements, it suffices to only consider set systems <math>W</math> such that every set in <math>W</math> has cardinality <math>k</math>, so often the sunflower lemma is equivalently phrased as holding for "<math>k</math>-uniform" set systems.{{sfnp|Alweiss|Lovett|Wu|Zhang|2020|p=3}}

=== Sunflower lemma ===

{{harvtxt|Erdős|Rado|1960|loc=p. 86}} proved the '''sunflower lemma''', which states that<ref>{{cite book |last=Kostochka |first=Alexandr V. | author-link = Alexandr Kostochka|contribution=Extremal Problems on Δ-Systems |date=2000 |title=Numbers, Information and Complexity |pages=143–150 |editor-last=Althöfer |editor-first=Ingo |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4757-6048-4_14 |isbn=978-1-4757-6048-4 |editor2-last=Cai |editor2-first=Ning |editor3-last=Dueck |editor3-first=Gunter |editor4-last=Khachatrian |editor4-first=Levon}}</ref>

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = <math>f(k,r)\le k!(r-1)^k.</math>
<!-- The actual Erdős-Rado paper gives k!(r-1)^{k+1}, presumably because they allow for duplicated sets in their set system. However, all modern cited sources I could find (Kalai blog post, Alweiss et al paper, Jukna's Extremal Combinatorics) all say that Erdos-Rado give k!(r-1)^k. I'm going with the recent sources over the original. -->

That is, if <math>k</math> and <math>r</math> are positive [[integers]], then a set system <math>W</math> of cardinality greater than <math>k!(r-1)^{k}</math> of sets of cardinality <math>k</math> contains a sunflower with at least <math>r</math> sets.
| name = sunflower lemma
| note = {{harvtxt|Erdős|Rado|1960|loc=p. 86}}
}}

{{Collapse top|title=Proof}}
{{Math proof
| title = Proof
| proof = The Erdős-Rado sunflower lemma can be proved directly through induction. First, <math>f(1,r)\le r-1</math>, since the set system <math>W</math> must be a collection of distinct sets of size one, and so <math>r</math> of these sets make a sunflower. In the general case, suppose <math>W</math> has no sunflower with <math>r</math> sets. Then consider <math>A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_t \in W</math> to be a maximal collection of pairwise disjoint sets (that is, <math>A_i \cap A_j</math> is the empty set unless <math>i = j</math>, and every set in <math>W</math> intersects with some <math>A_i</math>). Because we assumed that <math>W</math> had no sunflower of size <math>r</math>, and a collection of pairwise disjoint sets is a sunflower, <math>t < r</math>.

Let <math>A = A_1 \cup A_2 \cup \cdots \cup A_t</math>. Since each <math>A_i</math> has cardinality <math>k</math>, the cardinality of <math>A</math> is bounded by <math>kt \leq k(r-1)</math>. Define <math>W_a</math> for some <math>a \in A</math> to be

:<math>W_a = \{S \setminus \{a\} \mid a \in S,\, S \in W\}.</math>

Then <math>W_a</math> is a set system, like <math>W</math>, except that every element of <math>W_a</math> has <math>k-1</math> elements. Furthermore, every sunflower of <math>W_a</math> corresponds to a sunflower of <math>W</math>, simply by adding back <math>a</math> to every set. This means that, by our assumption that <math>W</math> has no sunflower of size <math>r</math>, the size of <math>W_a</math> must be bounded by <math>f(k-1,r)-1</math>.

Since every set <math>S \in W</math> intersects with one of the <math>A_i</math>'s, it intersects with <math>A</math>, and so it corresponds to at least one of the sets in a <math>W_a</math>:

:<math>|W| \leq \sum_{a \in A} |W_a| \leq |A| (f(k-1, r)-1) \leq k(r-1)f(k-1, r) - |A| \leq k(r-1)f(k-1, r) - 1.</math>

Hence, if <math>|W| \ge k(r-1)f(k-1,r)</math>, then <math>W</math> contains an <math>r</math> set sunflower of size <math>k</math> sets. Hence, <math>f(k,r) \le 
k(r-1)f(k-1,r)</math> and the theorem follows.<ref name="kalai"/>
}}
{{Collapse bottom}}

===Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture===

The '''sunflower conjecture''' is one of several variations of the conjecture of {{harvtxt|Erdős|Rado|1960|loc=p. 86}}  that for each <math>r>2</math>, <math>f(k,r)\le C^k</math> for some constant <math>C>0</math> depending only on <math>r</math>. The conjecture remains open even for fixed low values of <math>r</math>; for example <math>r=3</math>; it is not known whether <math>f(k,3)\le C^k</math> for some <math>C>0</math>.<ref name="Abbott">{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=H.L |last2=Hanson |first2=D |last3=Sauer |first3=N |title=Intersection theorems for systems of sets |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A |date=May 1972 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=381–389 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(72)90103-3 |doi-access=free }}</ref> A 2021 paper by Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, and Zhang gives the best progress towards the conjecture, proving that <math>f(k,r)\le C^k </math> for {{nowrap|<math>C = O(r^3\log(k)\log\log(k))</math>.{{sfnp|Alweiss|Lovett|Wu|Zhang|2020}}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/|title=Quanta Magazine - Illuminating Science|website=Quanta Magazine|access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref>}} A month after the release of the first version of their paper, Rao sharpened the bound to <math>C=O(r\log(rk))</math>;{{sfnp|Rao|2020}} the current best-known bound is <math>C=O(r\log k)</math>.{{sfnp|Bell|Chueluecha|Warnke|2021}}

===Sunflower lower bounds===
Erdős and Rado proved the following lower bound on <math>f(k,r)</math>. It is equal to the statement that the original sunflower lemma is optimal in <math>r</math>.

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = <math> (r-1)^k \le f(k,r). </math>
| name = Theorem
| note = lower bound on <math>f(k,r)</math>
}}

{{Math proof
| title = Proof
| proof = For <math> k = 1 </math> a set of <math>r-1</math> sequence of distinct elements is not a sunflower.
Let <math>h(k-1,r)</math> denote the size of the largest set of <math>k-1</math>-sets with no <math>r</math> sunflower. Let <math>H</math> be such a set. Take an additional set of <math>r-1</math> elements and add one element to each set in one of <math>r-1</math> disjoint copies of <math>H</math>. Take the union of the <math>r-1</math> disjoint copies with the elements added and denote this set <math>H^*</math>. The copies of <math>H</math> with an element added form an <math>r-1</math> partition of <math>H^*</math>. We have that,<math>(r-1)|H| \le |H^*|</math>. <math>H^*</math> is sunflower free since any selection of <math>r</math> sets if in one of the disjoint partitions is sunflower free by assumption of H being sunflower free. Otherwise, if <math>r</math> sets are selected from across multiple sets of the partition, then two must be selected from one partition since there are only <math>r-1</math> partitions. This implies that at least two sets and not all the sets will have an element in common. Hence this is not a sunflower of <math>r</math> sets.
}}

A stronger result is the following theorem:

{{Math theorem
| math_statement = <math>f(a+b,r) \ge (f(a,r)-1)(f(b,r)-1)</math>
| name = Theorem
| note = stronger lower bound
}}

{{Math proof
| title = Proof
| proof = Let <math>F</math> and <math>F^*</math> be two sunflower free families. For each set <math>A</math> in <math>F</math>, append every set in <math>F^*</math> to <math>A</math> to produce <math>|F^*|</math> many sets. Denote this family of sets <math>F_A</math>. Take the union of <math>F_A</math> over all <math>A</math> in <math>F</math>. This produces a family of <math>|F^*||F|</math> sets which is sunflower free.
}}

For <math>k = 2</math>, <math>f(k,r) = r(r-1)</math> if <math>r</math> is odd, and <math>(r-1)^2+r/2 - 1</math> if <math>r</math> is even. The only other known case outside of these determined families is for <math>k=3</math>, <math>r=3</math>, where <math>f(k,r)=20</math>.

The best existing lower bound for the Erdos-Rado Sunflower problem for <math> r=3 </math> is <math> 10^{k/2-O(\log k)} \le f(k,3) </math>, due to Abott, Hansen, and Sauer.<ref name="Abbott2">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Abbott | first1 = H. L.
 | last2 = Hanson | first2 = D.
 | last3 = Sauer | first3 = N.
 | doi = 10.1016/0097-3165(72)90103-3
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A]]
 | mr = 297579
 | pages = 381–389
 | title = Intersection theorems for systems of sets
 | volume = 12
 | year = 1972}}</ref> This bound has not been improved in over 50 years.

Below is a table of known lower bounds for smaller <math>r</math> and <math>k</math>:<ref name="Abbott" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abbott |first1=H. ==Weak sunflower conjecture==
Another version of the problem, sometimes called the '''weak sunflower conjecture''' or the '''Erdős–Szemerédi sunflower conjecture''', deals with the case where the family of sets is a subset of the [[power set]] of an ''n''-element set. In this version, the size of the individual sets is not restricted. The conjecture states that if <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is a family of subsets of <math>{1, 2, \ldots, n}</math> and <math>|\mathcal{F}| > c^n</math> for some constant <math>c<2</math>, then <math>\mathcal{F}</math> must contain a sunflower of size 3 (the case where <math>r=3</math>).

This conjecture was resolved as a consequence of a breakthrough on the [[cap set problem]]. [[Noga Alon|Alon]], [[Amir Shpilka|Shpilka]], and [[Chris Umans|Umans]] had previously shown that an exponential upper bound for the cap set problem would imply a solution to the weak sunflower conjecture for <math>r=3</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Alon
|first1=Noga
|last2=Shpilka
|first2=Amir
|last3=Umans
|first3=Chris
|title=On Sunflowers and Matrix Multiplication
|journal=Computational Complexity
|date=October 2013
|volume=22
|issue=2
|pages=219–243
|doi=10.1007/s00037-013-0060-1
|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220138268_On_Sunflowers_and_Matrix_Multiplication
}}</ref> In 2016, [[Jordan Ellenberg|Ellenberg]] and [[Dion Gijswijt|Gijswijt]], building on the work of [[Ernie Croot|Croot]], [[Vsevolod Lev|Lev]], and [[Péter Pach|Pach]], used [[polynomial method in combinatorics|polynomial methods]] to prove a tight exponential upper bound on the size of cap sets.<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Ellenberg
|first1=Jordan S.
|last2=Gijswijt
|first2=Dion
|title=On large subsets of <math>\mathbb{F}_q^n</math> with no three-term arithmetic progression
|journal=Annals of Mathematics
|volume=185
|issue=1
|year=2017
|pages=339-343
|doi=10.4007/annals.2017.185.1.8
|arxiv=1605.09223
}}</ref>

Following this, Eric Naslund and Will Sawin adapted these methods to provide an explicit proof for the weak sunflower conjecture. They proved that the size of any family of subsets of <math>{1, 2, \ldots, n}</math> without a 3-sunflower is at most <math>3n \sum_{k \le n/3} \tbinom{n}{k}</math>, which is bounded by <math>(1.89)^n</math> for large <math>n</math>. This confirmed the conjecture that such families have a size of at most <math>c^n</math> for a constant <math>c<2</math>.<ref>{{cite journal
|last1=Naslund
|first1=Eric
|last2=Sawin
|first2=Will
|title=Upper bounds for sunflower-free sets
|journal=Forum of Mathematics, Sigma
|year=2017
|volume=5
|pages=e15
|doi=10.1017/fms.2017.12
|arxiv=1606.09575
|doi-access=free
}}</ref>

== Weak sunflowers ==
A family of sets <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is called a '''weak sunflower''' (or weak &Delta;-system) if all pairwise intersections have the same ''size''. That is, there exists an integer <math>c \ge 0</math> such that for any two distinct sets <math>A, B \in \mathcal{F}</math>, it holds that <math>|A \cap B| = c</math>.

Every strong sunflower is, by definition, a weak sunflower. However, the converse is not always true. For a family to be a strong sunflower, the pairwise intersections must be the ''exact same set'', not just the same size. For example, consider the following family of four 3-uniform sets:
:<math>\mathcal{F} = \{\{1,2,3\}, \{1,4,5\}, \{1,6,7\}, \{2,4,6\}\}</math>
This family is a weak sunflower because every pair of sets has an intersection of size 1. However, it is not a strong sunflower because the intersections are not all identical.

If a weak sunflower is sufficiently large, it is ''forced'' to be a strong sunflower through the [[pigeonhole principle]]. Specifically, any <math>k</math>-uniform weak sunflower with more than <math>(r-2)\tbinom{k}{c}+1</math> sets must contain a strong sunflower with <math>r</math> petals.<ref name="Jukna2011">{{cite book 
|last=Jukna 
|first=Stasys 
|title=Extremal Combinatorics: With Applications in Computer Science 
|series=Texts in Theoretical Computer Science. An EATCS Series |date=2011 
|publisher=Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg 
|isbn=978-3-642-17364-6 
|pages=89–98 
|chapter=Sunflowers 
|doi=10.1007/978-3-642-17364-6_6}}</ref>

=== Relation to Ramsey's Theorem ===
By constructing a [[complete graph]] where vertices represent the sets and edges are colored by intersection size, [[Ramsey's theorem]] guarantees the existence of a large monochromatic clique, which corresponds to a weak sunflower the same size as the clique. So, for a case like <math>f(3,5)</math>, where a sunflower of size 5 using 3-uniform sets will always be both weak and strong, the ''multicolor Ramsey number'' <math>R(5,5,5)</math> serves as an upper bound for <math>f(3,5)</math>. While this method successfully proves the existence of sunflowers, the upper bounds it provides for the sunflower number <math>f(k,r)</math> are much weaker than those obtained from more direct combinatorial arguments.

==Applications of the sunflower lemma==

The sunflower lemma has numerous applications in [[theoretical computer science]]. For example, in 1986, Razborov used the sunflower lemma to prove that the Clique language required <math>n^{\log(n)}</math> (superpolynomial) size monotone circuits, a breakthrough result in [[circuit complexity]] theory at the time. Håstad, Jukna, and Pudlák used it to prove lower bounds on depth-<math>3</math> <math>AC_0</math> circuits. It has also been applied in the [[parameterized complexity]] of the [[Set cover problem|hitting set problem]], to design [[fixed-parameter tractable]] algorithms for finding small sets of elements that contain at least one element from a given family of sets.{{sfnp|Flum|Grohe|2006}}

==Analogue for infinite collections of sets==
A version of the '''<math>\Delta</math>-lemma''' which is essentially equivalent to the Erdős-Rado <math>\Delta</math>-system theorem states that a countable collection of k-sets contains a countably infinite sunflower or <math>\Delta</math>-system.

The '''<math>\Delta</math>-lemma''' states that every [[Uncountable set|uncountable]] collection of [[finite set]]s contains an uncountable <math>\Delta</math>-system.

The <math>\Delta</math>-lemma is a [[Combinatorics|combinatorial]] [[Set theory|set-theoretic]] tool used in proofs to impose an [[upper bound]] on the size of a collection of pairwise incompatible elements in a [[Forcing (set theory)|forcing]] [[Partially ordered set|poset]].  It may for example be used as one of the ingredients in a proof showing that it is consistent with [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]] that the [[continuum hypothesis]] does not hold. It was introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Nikolai Aleksandrovich Shanin|last=Shanin|year=1946}}.

If <math>W</math> is an <math>\omega_2</math>-sized collection of [[Countable set|countable]] subsets of <math>\omega_2</math>, and if the continuum hypothesis holds, then there is an <math>\omega_2</math>-sized <math>\Delta</math>-subsystem. Let <math>\langle A_\alpha:\alpha<\omega_2\rangle</math> enumerate <math>W</math>.  For <math>\operatorname{cf}(\alpha)=\omega_1</math>, let 
<math>f(\alpha) = \sup(A_\alpha \cap \alpha)</math>.  By [[Fodor's lemma]], fix <math>S</math> stationary in <math>\omega_2</math> such that <math>f</math> is constantly equal to <math>\beta</math> on <math>S</math>.
Build <math>S'\subseteq S</math> of [[cardinality]] <math>\omega_2</math> such that whenever <math>i < j</math> are in <math>S'</math> then <math>A_i \subseteq j</math>.  Using the continuum hypothesis, there are only <math>\omega_1</math>-many countable subsets of <math>\beta</math>, so by further thinning we may stabilize the kernel.

==Cap set problem==
The solution to the [[cap set problem]] can be used to prove a partial form of the sunflower conjecture, namely that if a family of subsets of an <math>n</math>-element set has no 3-sunflower (the case where <math>r=3</math>), then the number of subsets in the family is at most <math>c^n</math> for a constant <math>c<2</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-begin-to-tame-wild-sunflower-problem-20191021/|title=Mathematicians Begin to Tame Wild 'Sunflower' Problem|last=Hartnett|first=Kevin|website=Quanta Magazine|date=21 October 2019 |access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref><ref name="bulletin">{{cite journal|last=Grochow | first = Joshua A. | doi = 10.1090/bull/1648 | volume = 56 | journal = Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society | mr = 3886143 | pages = 29–64 | title = New applications of the polynomial method: The cap set conjecture and beyond | year = 2019 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/2016/05/17/polymath-10-emergency-post-5-the-erdos-szemeredi-sunflower-conjecture-is-now-proven/|title=Polymath 10 Emergency Post 5: The Erdos-Szemeredi Sunflower Conjecture is Now Proven|first=Gil|last=Kalai|author-link=Gil Kalai|date=May 17, 2016|work=Combinatorics and more}}.</ref>
